Introducing 'The Second Order', a new monthly newsletter on the systems, shifts, and forces redefining workplace learning. The first of those shifts is already underway, and none of it registers as a problem. The learning function is still doing exactly the job it was built for, and that job was defined when producing learning was slow, expensive and dependent on scarce expertise. AI has removed all three of those constraints, leaving a function that can hit every one of its KPIs and still be aimed at a target the business has moved past. The Second Order follows shifts like that one from the point they begin to the point they force a decision. Subscribe to our newsletter for more insights.

Daqstra is the AI-native operating layer for complex hardware teams, helping engineers connect every instrument, understand every test, and safely run what comes next. Great hardware is built through cycles of testing, failure, and discovery, and testing infrastructure shouldn’t bottleneck that engineering. Yet teams across aerospace, energy, and robotics assemble test setups from NI systems, PLCs, vendor software, custom electronics, and in-house code that were never designed to work together. Engineers end up rebuilding integrations, searching across machines, and reconstructing what happened before they can learn from a test. Founders Anchit Kumar and Darell Chua built Daqstra after experiencing this firsthand while firing liquid rocket engines in the Mojave. Daqstra records commands, telemetry, configurations, and engineering context in one system, giving its AI the context to compare runs, trace anomalies back to source data, and help prepare repeatable test sequences through a controlled API. Instead of stopping at a summary, Daqstra closes the loop from observation to the next test while engineers remain in control. Daqstra is now used day-to-day in active aerospace programs and has signed an industrial energy pilot targeting $100K+ in annual savings. If you lead test, integration, propulsion, or validation at a complex hardware company, Daqstra wants to hear from you. Congrats on the launch, Anchit and Darell! 🚀 https://lnkd.in/gdSrABY7

Darell Chua and I started Y Combinator this week! Two days in, and what's stuck with me is the people. Everyone here has a story, and every person I've met has pushed me in some unique way. My favorite part has been hearing the partners talk through their own founder journeys (definitely not biased but Gustaf Alströmer 🇺🇦 's is my personal favorite). I realized how much of what they went through still holds true today. Darell and I met building rocket engines in college. We'd drive out to the Mojave Desert to test them, and the hardest part was always all the equipment around the test – not the actual test. The rocket science turned out to be in capturing the data, controlling the hardware or catching a failure before it took the whole stand. All of it manual, fragile, held together by hand. When we built the first prototype for Daqstra , we were just college students in a messy campus basement. We built the infrastructure that runs hardware tests – for rockets, satellites, and anything physical – so teams can move fast and trust what they measure. We started building it because we needed it ourselves. And we made it AI-native so that the story behind what engineers are building is not lost and actually pushes the process forward. We met through our love for space exploration and our dedication to making technology that enables us to reach the stars. We now want to help the companies at the frontier of doing that. At YC I haven't just seen companies. I've seen strong stories and people who aren't held down by conventional beliefs. People driven to figure it out as they go. We know engineers like this are out there too and we want to help them do what they do best. Build the future.

What a way to end the year with a bang! Last week, I presented my Senior Design project for the UCSD Chemical Plant and Process Design course with my group mates, Mia Ge , Justin Chen , and Jasper Zhang , where we were awarded a Distinguished Poster Award by the Engineering Team at EMD Electronics, based in Carlsbad. For six months, we designed and optimized a chemical plant for EMD Electronics to manufacture a silane-derived molecule used in the semiconductor and integrated circuit industry. Our process was designed using Aspen Plus software, which came with plenty of challenges on its own. Throughout this project, I learned about equipment sizing, distillation optimization, and the financial motivations which play a large role in design. I especially enjoyed learning about plant safety, hazard prevention, and the federal and state regulations which govern these processes. We learned the importance of the first canon of the AIChE code of ethics, to “Hold paramount the safety, health, and welfare of the public and protect the environment in performance of professional duties”. Later that evening, we were reminded of these principles at the Jacobs School of Engineering Ring Ceremony, where our graduating senior engineering class affirmed our oath of integrity. Thank you to my professors, Ben Russ and Alyssa Powell for showing us the ropes! I also want to give a special thank you to Anthony Lachawiec Jr, PhD, PE, CIH, CSP, CCPSC for your technical guidance and teaching. And thank you, Jocelyn Beltran Leon , for your inspiration and mentorship!

Stoked to announce that we will be joining Y Combinator 's Summer 2026 batch! Building Daqstra so far has been some of the most exciting work I've done – from late nights in the Mojave to long hours debugging alongside the team. Along the way, one thing has become increasingly clear: as AI moves deeper into the physical world, it will need software that can understand, model, and reason about complex engineering systems. That’s the problem we’re driven to solve at Daqstra. That's why we're moving to San Francisco to build it — and I couldn't be more excited for what's ahead. Special thanks to all the friends and family who stuck through it (you know who you are) — and especially my dad, Avinash Kumar for backing me on every decision, even the risky ones. Big thanks to Gustaf Alströmer 🇺🇦 for taking a shot on us!

Last week, I completed the Spring Fellowship with AI Alignment at UC San Diego . Special thanks to Aldan Creo and Kevin Zhang for organizing this! It was a valuable experience to discuss, question, and think through one of the most pressing problems in technology today: how do we build AI systems that are not just powerful, but reliable, interpretable, and aligned with human intent? AI is probably gonna become one of the most influential technologies of our lifetimes. But despite how useful these systems already are, we still do not fully understand how they represent our world internally, why they make certain decisions, or how they will behave when given more autonomy across real products and institutions. This matters because the hard part is not only making models smarter - its making sure they do what we actually mean. As a naive example, if a CEO asks an advanced GPT 10 that is integrated everywhere to cut compute costs, what if it just nukes the database? (has happened btw) Even more pressing - what if a random website the AI consults is prompt-injected to do some harmful stuff? We don't have a real solution to that either. In a real company, hospital, financial system, or government workflow, this becomes a serious product and engineering problem. That is why alignment cannot just be treated as abstract philosophy. It is also about better engineering: guardrails, evaluations, interpretability, observability, accountability, human oversight, and careful product design. Frontier labs like OpenAI and Anthropic have made impressive progress here, but then as AI gets integrated into nearly every tool used by individuals, companies, and governments, I think alignment will become one of the bigger bottlenecks to realizing the upside of this technology. The fellowship helped me see AI alignment less as a distant theoretical concern and more as a practical question worth thinking about: How do we build systems and products that are capable enough to be useful, but constrained and understandable enough to be trusted? #AI #UCSanDiego

What started as a curiosity for flight, engineering, and the unknown has become a journey I am incredibly grateful for. Today, I am excited to share a few milestones: I graduated with Highest Honors from the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign with a B.S. in Aerospace Engineering and a Minor in Computer Science. I also graduated from Parkland College with a Certificate in Aviation, and as part of that program, I passed my Private Pilot examinations and am now officially a licensed private pilot. So yes, after studying aerospace engineering for four years, I finally earned the chance to be the one behind the controls. I am also thrilled to share that after receiving offers from Carnegie Mellon University , the University of Pennsylvania , Purdue University , and the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign across Aerospace Engineering and Robotics programs, I have chosen to continue my journey at the Carnegie Mellon University Robotics Institute within the Carnegie Mellon University School of Computer Science , where I will be pursuing a research-based Master of Science in Robotics. I am excited for the opportunity to keep learning, building, and growing at the intersection of engineering, autonomy, and robotics. I am deeply grateful to my professors, mentors, family, friends, and everyone who has supported me through this chapter. Aerospace Engineering at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign has shaped me in more ways than I can put into one post, which is probably for the best because this post is already getting dangerously close to essay length. I am especially thankful for the opportunities I had to work on aerospace systems, robotics, and research that continually pushed me to think across disciplines. Next stop: Pittsburgh. Very excited for what lies ahead at CMU Robotics.

Finishing college a couple weeks ago has given me time to reflect on my last semester. Final year is a strange thing. You're simultaneously trying to finish strong academically, tie up everything you've built over four years, and figure out what comes next - often all in the same week. But the moment I keep coming back to is being named a gradireland Female Leadership Undergraduate of the Year 2026 Finalist. Out of 7,100+ applicants nationally, across ten categories. I didn't win. But being in that room, being considered in that company, is something I'll carry for a long time. 🙏🏻✨ Thank you to everyone at gradireland and Deloitte for this recognition, and to everyone at the University of Limerick and Kemmy Business School for everything that led me into that room. #GradIreland #UGOTY2026 #FemaleLeadership #UniversityOfLimerick #KemmyBusinessSchool
